subject: physiology
title: The Carotid Body, Pulmonary Reflexes, and Periodic Breathing

steps.tx: Peripheral arterial chemoreception is mediated predominantly by paired sensory neurovascular organs located at the bifurcation of common carotid arteries. Each **carotid body** possesses the highest blood flow per unit tissue weight in the entire human body, reaching two thousand millilitres per hundred grams per minute, allowing continuous monitoring of dissolved arterial blood gases.
steps.say: Carotid bodies have the highest blood flow per gram of tissue, allowing instant detection of changes in arterial blood gases.

left.title: Carotid Body Chemoreceptors
points: Located at common carotid artery bifurcation
Afferent sensory transmission via Hering nerve to CN IX
Also stimulated by hypercapnia and acidosis

right.title: Aortic Body Chemoreceptors
points: Located along superior and inferior aortic arch
Afferent sensory transmission via vagus nerve (CN X)
Smaller ventilatory influence than carotid bodies

steps.tx: Chemosensory transduction in carotid bodies resides in dopamine-rich **glomus type I cells**, which synapse directly upon sensory nerve endings of the glossopharyngeal nerve. When arterial oxygen partial pressure drops below sixty millimetres of mercury, oxygen-sensitive potassium channels close, inducing cellular depolarization and calcium-dependent neurotransmitter release.
steps.say: Glomus type one cells depolarize when oxygen drops below sixty millimetres of mercury, releasing neurotransmitters to activate glossopharyngeal afferents.

steps.tx: Over-inflation of the pulmonary parenchyma is prevented by the protective **Hering-Breuer reflex**. When tidal volume exceeds one litre during strenuous exercise, slowly adapting pulmonary stretch receptors in bronchial smooth muscle fire, sending inhibitory vagal impulses to the dorsal respiratory group to terminate inspiration abruptly.
steps.say: The Hering-Breuer reflex uses pulmonary stretch receptors to switch off inspiration when lungs inflate beyond one litre.

steps.tx: Unmyelinated sensory C-fibre endings situated within alveolar walls adjacent to pulmonary capillaries are known as **juxtacapillary J receptors**. Engorgement of pulmonary microvessels or interstitial fluid accumulation in heart failure stimulates J receptors via the vagus nerve, eliciting rapid shallow tachypnoea and dyspnoea.
steps.say: Juxtacapillary J receptors detect pulmonary congestion, sending vagal signals that cause rapid shallow breathing and shortness of breath.

steps.tx: A classic oscillatory respiratory rhythm characterized by waxing and waning tidal volumes separated by central apnoeic pauses is designated **Cheyne-Stokes breathing**. It occurs characteristically in severe congestive heart failure and bilateral cortical brain injury, driven by delayed circulatory transport time between the lungs and brainstem chemoreceptors.
steps.say: Cheyne-Stokes breathing features alternating crescendo-decrescendo hyperpnoea and central apnoea caused by circulatory transit delays.

left.title: Cheyne-Stokes Respirations
points: Smooth crescendo-decrescendo tidal volumes with apnoeic pauses
Prolonged lung-to-brain circulation time in severe heart failure
Chemoreceptors continuously overshoot and undershoot ventilation
Seen also in bilateral hemispheric stroke and high altitude

right.title: Biot Breathing (Ataxic)
points: Completely irregular breaths of variable depth interspersed with apnoea
Direct damage to dorsal respiratory group in medulla
Associated with severe raised intracranial pressure and herniation

steps.tx: During high-altitude exposure, hypoxic hyperventilation induces respiratory alkalosis, causing unstable feedback loops that generate nocturnal **periodic breathing**. These periodic oscillations severely disrupt restful sleep architecture until renal bicarbonate excretion compensates over several days or acetazolamide is administered to stimulate central metabolic acidosis.
steps.say: Nocturnal periodic breathing occurs at high altitudes due to hypocapnic alkalosis, which destabilizes the central respiratory drive.

rows: Severe heart failure or bilateral cortical lesions
Irregular chaotic gasps with variable pauses
Direct medullary damage; impending brainstem herniation
Severe metabolic ketoacidosis or lactic acidosis
Lower pontine tegmental lesions transecting pneumotaxic tract

steps.tx: Voluntary cessation of respiration is constrained by the physiological **breath holding breaking point**. When arterial carbon dioxide partial pressure climbs to approximately fifty millimetres of mercury, intense stimulation of central and peripheral chemoreceptors overcomes voluntary cortical inhibition, forcing the individual to resume spontaneous breathing.
steps.say: The breath holding breaking point occurs when arterial carbon dioxide rises to fifty millimetres of mercury, forcing involuntary breathing.

Breaking Point Reached: Involuntary Medullary Drive Overrides Cerebral Cortex

steps.tx: If an underwater swimmer hyperventilates beforehand, profound hypocapnia suppresses the urge to breathe without significantly increasing total stored oxygen. During subsequent underwater exertion, oxygen drops to fatal levels before carbon dioxide reaches the breaking point, precipitating sudden **shallow water blackout** and silent drowning.
steps.say: Prior hyperventilation delays the carbon dioxide breaking point, causing sudden fatal loss of consciousness underwater.
